claims.text: Successful formation of homogeneous noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by an optimized rapid thermal profile.
Rapid high-temperature processing can cause near-simultaneous decomposition and reduction of multiple metal precursors.
The high-temperature stage enables rapid atomic mixing of the constituent metals.
Rapid cooling freezes a mixed, non-equilibrium high-entropy state and suppresses secondary-phase formation.
Rapid cooling suppresses the diffusional processes required for phase separation.
Differences in precursor reduction rates and atomic mobilities intrinsically cause elemental segregation when the thermal profile is not optimized.
The initial material consists of five or more noble- and transition-metal salts dispersed on a substrate or in a confined medium.
Relevant processing conditions are temperatures around or above 1500–2000 K applied on millisecond timescales.
Kinetic factors dominate under the proposed extreme-temperature, short-duration conditions.
The proposed process produces nanoscale, homogeneous solid-solution particles with uniformly distributed elements.
The resulting nanoparticles retain high surface-atom exposure or high surface-area characteristics.
Tailoring the rapid thermal profile yields controlled nanoparticle size.
Tailoring the rapid thermal profile minimizes phase separation and elemental segregation.
A standard rapid thermal treatment without tailored ramp and cooling control typically produces inconsistent, phase-separated, or segregated products.
The mechanism is intended to apply to shock-based or rapid thermal processing of noble-metal and transition-metal systems at extreme temperatures.
The mechanism may not apply to low-temperature solution syntheses because their kinetic and entropic contributions differ.
The optimal temperature and time window varies with the particular elemental combination.
The substrate or support can restrict applicability or complicate alloy formation.
Ru-Ni nanoparticles phase-separate at approximately 1500 K for 500 ms, and the cited calculation places their alloy-formation requirement at at least 2000 K.
Ru-based four- and five-element nanoparticles were reported to contain uniformly distributed elements without segregation or immiscible phases.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule frames the thermal profile alone as governing alloy formation, whereas the uncertainty field states that the required window depends on elemental identity and that substrate or support interactions can also affect the result. A failed improvement could therefore reflect those acknowledged dependencies rather than decisively falsifying the thermal mechanism alone.
